analysis.one_liner: Adds roughly $90 billion to IRS enforcement and technology, aimed at auditing high earners and big corporations.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced with 40 Democratic cosponsors in July 2026 and referred to the House Appropriations Committee, where it has received no further action.
analysis.plain_summary: The Stop CHEATERS Act would give the IRS dedicated money for six years to hire and keep auditors who can handle high-income individuals and large corporations, upgrade the agency's outdated computers, and improve services for everyday filers. It would also require the IRS to report regularly on how it is shifting audit resources toward the top of the income scale, and require an independent Inspector General to evaluate whether that plan is working. The money is directed at collecting taxes already owed under current law, not raising anyone's tax rate.
analysis.who_benefits: Honest taxpayers at every income level, because the bill targets the roughly hundreds of billions in taxes that go uncollected each year, much of it owed by high earners and large corporations. Ordinary filers also benefit from more IRS customer-service funding, which means faster help with filing and refunds.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Ordinary taxpayers and everyone who pays what they owe

how_it_helps.text: The bill provides $3.6 billion in FY2026 rising to $12.2 billion in FY2031 for IRS tax enforcement, explicitly to determine and collect owed taxes and to conduct criminal investigations of tax and financial crimes.

It directs the IRS to recruit and retain auditors with the skills needed to audit high-income individuals and large corporations, and to report to Congress every two years on progress shifting enforcement resources toward them.

It funds taxpayer services (about $1.4-1.7 billion a year), which pays for pre-filing help, filing and account services, and taxpayer advocacy — the part of the IRS ordinary people actually interact with.
It requires a periodic analysis of how much uncollected tax comes from taxpayers at different income levels, creating a public, independent check on whether enforcement is really reaching the top.

It appropriates money for technology upgrades and fraud detection, and for business systems modernization — the IRS's aging computer systems have long been cited as a reason audits of complex returns are hard to do.

analysis.who_pays: High-income individuals and large corporations who currently underpay, who would face a greater chance of being audited and of having to pay taxes already owed. Indirectly, complex-return filers face higher preparation costs, and the spending itself is federal money that could go elsewhere.
analysis.who_pays_short: High earners and corporations that underpay taxes

drawbacks.text: The bill appropriates roughly $90 billion over six years with no offsetting revenue in the bill text itself, so its net fiscal benefit depends on how much additional tax the enforcement actually collects — an amount the IRS has historically struggled to guarantee.

More enforcement funding does not automatically mean more audits of the wealthy: IRS audits are cheapest per return for low-income earners (such as those claiming the Earned Income Tax Credit) because they are simple, and the bill addresses this only through a reporting requirement, not a binding floor.
Money 'available until expended' can sit unspent or be redirected by future appropriations choices, so the dollar amounts are not a guarantee of results.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is favorable if the enforcement money works: most independent analyses find each dollar spent auditing complex high-income returns returns several dollars in collected tax, and the bill pairs enforcement with service funding that helps ordinary filers. The real weaknesses are that it is appropriations money rather than enforceable policy (a future Congress could undo it), and that it nudges rather than requires the IRS to prioritize the wealthy over easier-to-audit low-income returns.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on July 16, 2026 and referred to the House Appropriations Committee, which has not scheduled any action on it; with the session ending January 3, 2027, it sits with no markup or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Suzan DelBene introduced the bill on July 16, 2026 with 40 Democratic cosponsors, all from her own party, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Appropriations.

The bill provides six years of additional IRS appropriations — enforcement, taxpayer services, technology, and systems modernization — and requires biennial reports to Congress on shifting audits toward high earners and large corporations, evaluated by the Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration.
No committee markup, floor action, or vote has occurred; the only actions on record are introduction and committee referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High-income individuals and large corporations that underpay taxes benefit, since the enforcement funding never advanced; the status quo of uneven audit resources remains in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who avoid extra IRS scrutiny

for.name: Rep. Suzan DelBene

for.role: Cosponsors, including Ways and Means members Rep. Sewell, Rep. Larson, Rep. Chu, and Rep. Khanna
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors; none from the other party.

against.name: House Committee on Appropriations
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by the majority party
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on July 16, 2026 and has taken no further action — no markup, no subcommittee action, no advancement.

sides.party_line_note: All 41 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats with no Republican support on record, and the Republican-controlled referral committee has not moved it.

industries.industry: High-income individuals and large corporations that underpay taxes
industries.note: The bill's stated purpose is to shift audit resources toward these taxpayers and collect taxes already owed. Its interests here run against ordinary taxpayers, who otherwise effectively subsidize the gap through other taxes or unmet public spending.

industries.industry: Tax preparation, tax shelter, and high-end tax advisory services
industries.note: Better-funded IRS enforcement and modernized fraud detection raise the cost and risk of aggressive avoidance strategies sold to wealthy clients and businesses. Wealthy clients would face higher preparation and legal costs if audited.

industries.industry: Taxpayer service and tax administration technology vendors
industries.note: The bill directs billions into business systems modernization and technology upgrades, much of which flows to contractors that build and maintain IRS systems. That same spending is what makes enforcement of the well-off feasible, so the public interest and the vendors' interests align here.

analysis.trajectory: A standalone appropriations bill referred to the House Appropriations Committee late in a session, with no Republican cosponsors and no scheduled markup, almost never advances. The realistic path is that it dies when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027, unless its provisions are folded into a broader government funding bill, which would require majority-party support it does not have.
